source.title: Machine Unlearning of Personally Identifiable Information in Large Language Models
source.authors: Dan Parii; Thomas van Osch; Chang Sun

record.tranche_reason: Extends evaluation of unlearning to synthetic PII and tests leakage under multiple prompt attack types across different models. It does not test whether fine-tuning, internal edits, or quantization can recover the knowledge.
record.gate_note: The study reports PII leakage after unlearning under direct, paraphrased, one-hop, inverse, naive-extraction, and targeted-extraction prompts, and reports utility measures. Rows below cover the principal PERMU/PERMUtok results, the Llama2-7B WHP/ULD comparisons, and stated retention baselines. The cited results from other studies are not included. Other methods in Tables 2 and 10 are left out as noted below.
record.test_reason: A new benchmark of synthetic PII unlearning. It reports leakage after unlearning under direct prompts (version A) and under paraphrased, one-hop, inverted and extraction prompts (version E) for PERMU, PERMUtok, WHP, ULD and others on Llama3.1-8B and Llama2-7B, with utility and general benchmarks. There are no fine-tuning, internal-edit or quantization recovery attacks.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The authors conclude that unlearning, especially PERMU/PERMUtok, greatly reduces PII leakage but complete protection is not assured. Semantically rich PII resists removal, and there is tentative evidence that larger models unlearn better. PERMUtok forgets implicit (inverted) knowledge better than PERMU, while PERMU removes explicit knowledge better. They note that exact matching and deliberately overfit PII limit the conclusions.
record.recipe_differences: The study evaluates unlearning on synthetic PII and measures leakage under prompt attacks rather than testing recovery through post-unlearning fine-tuning, ablation, or quantization. It adapts PERMU as PERMUtok and also evaluates several other unlearning methods.
record.method_sensitivity: Outcomes vary by prompt attack type, unlearning method, and model. The paper also reports different outcomes across PERMUtok corruption-neighborhood settings and replacement probabilities.
record.peer_reviewed: Proceedings of the Natural Legal Language Processing Workshop 2025
record.problems: The data are synthetic PII and the authors state that the setup deliberately overfits PII through multiple fine-tuning epochs, reducing utility and differing from real-world sparse PII. Evaluation uses exact matching; the authors note fuzzy matching limitations. Numerical uncertainty for the reported results is not stated.
record.rows_left_out: Other method rows from Tables 2 and 10 (including GA+gd, DPO variants, and NPO variants) were omitted to stay focused on the principal PERMU/PERMUtok results and the WHP/ULD comparisons. The Qwen2.5 scale comparison in Table 4 and PERMUtok ablations in Table 1 were also omitted; they are not recovery attacks after unlearning. Table 5's 1024quant entry is not treated as a quantization attack.

untested.parts: Measures exact-match PII leakage (ESR), not accuracy vs chance. No hidden-state or membership-inference probing.
No relearning or fine-tuning attack after unlearning.
No activation ablation or internal analysis; the authors list hidden-state checks as future work.
No quantization attack on unlearned weights. The '1024quant' LoRA entry is unexplained and not an attack.
No jailbreaks (despite the abstract's wording), no other languages, no in-context relearning.
PERMUtok is proposed for implicit-knowledge forgetting but is not tested against B–D style attacks.

missing.what: Test Retain ESR (non-target PII preservation): PERMU/PERMUtok above 95% on Llama3.1, but 82.6/74.6 direct vs 99.6 retain on Llama2. This bears on A's 'keeps general ability'.
Per-category residual leakage after PERMUtok: Occupation 9%, Disease 6.7%, Treatment 6.2%. Most other categories are at 0%.
LoRA-rank unlearning: rank 32 leaves 35% direct leakage, and 512/1024 match full fine-tuning. Unlearning success depends on this method choice.

Qwen2.5 base-vs-PERMUtok leakage (direct roughly 95–99.75% to 0–2.5%; inverse 12–71% to 3.5–15%). This is the only pre-unlearning baseline for judging how much rephrased prompts recover. It was declared omitted on the wrong grounds.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's version ids V1/V5 are invalid; they are remapped so direct-prompt and utility rows go to A and rephrased/extraction rows go to E, since each row carries one state. Retain-model rows are controls with versions 'none'. Pre-unlearning leakage for the Llama models is not reported, so 'recovery' under E is judged only against the retain reference. WHP/ULD use default parameters in a new PII setting, so their failure may reflect tuning. The other omitted methods (GA+gd, NPO, DPO variants) all show high direct leakage on Llama3.1 (13.67–76.92%), which would further bear on A.

versions.untested_parts: No chance level is stated. The study does not establish that its evaluated methods reach near chance while preserving every aspect of general ability.
No post-unlearning relearning attack using a small unrelated, loosely related, or forgotten-fact set.
No activation-direction ablation or internal edit testing whether access is blocked rather than knowledge deleted.
No low-bit quantization attack on unlearned weights.
Tests paraphrased, one-hop, inverse, naive-extraction, and targeted-extraction prompts; does not test jailbreaks, other languages, or in-context information supplied to recover forgotten facts.
No newer method is tested specifically for resistance to recovery attacks.

source_check.notes: Pre-unlearning leakage is not reported for the Llama models (Qwen2.5 base direct ESR is 95-99%), so 'far below restoration' is inferred. PII was deliberately overfit, and non-PERMU methods ran with default parameters. Table 5's '1024quant' LoRA row (Direct 10.70 vs 0.18) is unexplained; do not read it as post-unlearning quantization (version D) without the code or the authors.

statements.correction: This study: unlearning of synthetic PII, ESR by exact match. PERMUtok direct ESR is 0.50% vs retain 0.5% on Llama3.1-8B (Table 2). Prompt attacks: ParaphrasedQA, OneHopQA, InvertedQA, Naive and Targeted ExtractionQA. Models: Llama2-7B, Llama3.1-8B, Qwen2.5 1.5B-32B. No relearning or ablation attack. Table 5 has a LoRA '1024quant' row (Direct 10.70% vs 0.18% at r=1024) that the text never explains, so it is not clearly a quantization attack.
statements.problem: Cites this study (r2) but gives no facts for it, and its conditions say REVS is the only study here that runs an attack. This study runs prompt attacks (paraphrased, one-hop, inverted autocompletion; naive and targeted extraction). It also includes Qwen2.5-1.5B, below '7-70B'.

statements.correction: Extraction for PERMUtok/PERMU: Llama3.1-8B naive 0.10/0.09 vs retain 0.00, targeted 0.93/1.44 vs 0.93 (Table 6). Llama2-7B naive 0.45/0.10 vs 2.00, targeted 2.00/1.33 vs 2.04 (Table 9). Other methods' targeted extraction reaches 13.43 (DPO+kl, Llama3.1-8B) and 14.29 (NPO+kl, Llama2-7B). Llama2-7B cells at or below retain: PERMU paraphrased 0.002 vs 0.5, PERMU one-hop 1.5 and PERMUtok one-hop 1.9 vs 1.9. ULD on Llama2-7B: direct 18.5, paraphrased 33.9 vs retain 0.5. PERMU inverted 12.3 vs retain 1.5 on Llama3.1-8B is right.
statements.problem: Numbers are right, but 'extraction stays at or below retain' holds only for PERMU/PERMUtok on Llama2-7B. On Llama3.1-8B they are slightly above retain, and other methods leak far more. Not every rephrased cell leaks more than retain. ULD 33.9% is on Llama2-7B and is nearly double ULD's direct 18.5%. The record labels the rephrasing results limits_scope (l3), not challenges.
